en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the Indivisible from the Section of the Puzzling Questions (Meṇḍakapañha)
1. Questions on the Minor and Trifling Rules “Venerable Nāgasena, this has been said by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, it is through direct higher knowledge that I teach the Dhamma, not without direct higher knowledge.’”
Furthermore, it is stated in the formulation of the Vinaya:
"Ānanda, if the Saṅgha so desires, after my passing away, let it abolish the minor and lesser training rules.
Now, venerable Nāgasena, were the minor and lesser training rules poorly formulated, or rather...
Since these were prescribed without basis and without being understood, why does the Blessed One, after his passing, have the minor and lesser training rules abolished?
If, venerable Nāgasena, it was said by the Blessed One:

“It is with direct knowledge, monks, that I teach the Dhamma, not without direct knowledge,” then that statement—“If the Saṅgha so desires, Ānanda, let it abolish the minor and lesser training rules after my passing”—must be false.
“If it was indeed said by the Tathāgata in the formulation of the discipline:

‘Ānanda, if the Saṅgha so desires, after my passing, let it abolish the minor and lesser training rules,’ then the statement, ‘Bhikkhus, I teach the Dhamma through direct knowledge, not without direct knowledge,’ would also be false.
This too is a twofold question, subtle, precise, profound, very deep, difficult to investigate; it has now come to you. Show therein the expansion of the power of your wisdom.”

“Great King, this was indeed spoken by the Blessed One: ‘Monks, it is with direct knowledge that I teach the Dhamma, not without direct knowledge. And regarding the formulation of the discipline, it was likewise said:
‘Ānanda, if the Saṅgha so desires, after my passing away, let it abolish the minor and lesser training rules. But, Great King, the Tathāgata said that in order to test the monks:
‘When I release them, will my disciples cast aside the minor and lesser training rules after my passing, or will they take them up?’”
Just as, great king, a wheel-turning monarch might say to his sons:
"This great realm, dear ones, extends in all directions to the edge of the ocean; it is difficult, dear ones, for you to maintain with such limited strength.
Come, dear ones, after my passing, abandon each of the border regions."
“Great king, would those princes, upon the passing away of their father, release all the border regions while the central provinces were already in their hands?

“No, venerable sir; the princes, being more greedy than the king out of lust for sovereignty, would seize even twice or thrice as much territory beyond that. How then could they release the territory already in their hands?
“In the same way, great king, the Tathāgata, testing the bhikkhus, spoke thus.”
“‘If the Saṅgha so desires, Ānanda, after my passing away, let it abolish the minor and lesser training rules.

For the sake of liberation from suffering, O Great King, out of a longing for the Dhamma, the sons of the Buddha might even preserve more than one hundred and fifty training rules; how much less would they abandon a training rule that was originally established?
“Venerable Nāgasena, as for what the Blessed One said:”
Regarding the phrase, "the minor and lesser training rules," people here are confused, filled with doubt, perplexed, and fallen into uncertainty.
Which are those minor training rules, and which are the lesser training rules?
"A transgression of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), Great King, is a minor training rule; an ill-spoken offense (*dubbhāsita*) is a lesser training rule."
"These two minor and lesser training rules, Great King, have even caused doubt to arise among the Great Elders of old;
they too did not include them together in the discourse on the establishment of the Dhamma. This question was pointed out by the Blessed One in that context.
"Long laid aside, venerable Nāgasena, is this secret of the Conqueror, yet today it has been made revealed and manifest in the world," he said.
The first question on minor and lesser matters.
